ClinicalDocument.title: SYNTHETIC RECORD, NOT A REAL MEDICAL RECORD — Psychiatry (mood disorders) Consultation — Paul Robeson

code.originalText: Psychiatric consultation and review: diagnosis of recurrent major depression, bipolar screening, start of sertraline and behavioral activation

text.paragraph: Probable severe major depression in a 58-year-old singer and actor under sustained political persecution, with passive thoughts of death. Please confirm the diagnosis with a structured interview, screen for bipolar disorder, judge suicide risk and the level of care, and advise on treatment, including when ECT or other treatments would be indicated. [S]

Urgency: Urgent, within three days. He has passive thoughts of being better off dead on several days, without intent, plan, preparation or past attempt. A safety plan is in place, there is no firearm at home, his medicines are locked, and he has the 988 Suicide & Crisis Lifeline in his phone. He has been told to call or text 988 or go to the nearest emergency department if the thoughts become active. [S]

list.item: Does he meet criteria for recurrent major depression, and is there any sign of bipolar disorder or psychotic features?
How should his concern about surveillance be understood in the assessment?
Can he be treated safely as an outpatient, and what should the safety plan include?
Which psychotherapy and which first antidepressant do you advise, and how should response be measured?
What is the plan if the first or second antidepressant trial fails?
When would ECT be indicated, and what would modern ECT and its alternatives involve for him?

text.paragraph: Mr. Robeson, a 58-year-old singer, actor and civil rights activist trained in law, is seen at the request of Dr. Bankole-Ashworth three days after his first visit. He describes about three months of low mood, exhaustion, early waking, poor appetite and loss of interest, with withdrawal from friends and from singing. He had a first depression about two years ago, after prostate surgery, that lifted slowly over some months without treatment. Before it he had some weeks of intense, absorbed work, sleeping his usual hours, without elation, irritability, racing thoughts, spending or other risky behavior. He has thoughts on some days that he would be better off dead, without intent or plan, and has never attempted suicide. He has lost most of his work and income, cannot travel abroad, and believes his telephone is listened to. He asked who would see this note and was told. [S]
Historical basis. These claims are historical evidence, not findings from a modern examination.

list.item: Paul Leroy Robeson was born on April 9, 1898, in Princeton, New Jersey. [D]
His father, the Rev. William Drew Robeson, was a minister, and his mother was Maria Louisa Bustill. [D]

In 1915 he was awarded a four-year academic scholarship to Rutgers, where he was elected to Phi Beta Kappa and graduated as valedictorian in 1919; he had been named to college All-America football teams. [D]
In 1923 he earned a law degree from Columbia Law School. [D]
In 1950 the State Department cancelled his passport, saying his overseas travel was 'contrary to the best interests of the United States'. [D]

He was blacklisted: his concerts were cancelled, record companies stopped recording him, his name was struck from the All-America teams and newsreel footage of him was destroyed, and his yearly income fell from more than $150,000 to less than $3,000. [D]

In 1956 he was called before the House Un-American Activities Committee, where he invoked the Fifth Amendment and closed by saying, 'You gentlemen belong with the Alien and Sedition Acts, and you are the nonpatriots, and you are the un-Americans, and you ought to be ashamed of yourselves.' [D]
His biographer Martin Duberman describes his first breakdown in 1955, after health problems related to prostate surgery: a period of intense, driven energy that was followed by a deep depression. [D]
A writer reviewing the Duberman biography has argued that he had the classic symptoms of bipolar disorder; no formal diagnosis of bipolar disorder in his lifetime is quoted. [R]

text.paragraph: No results recorded at this visit.

list.item: Major depressive disorder, recurrent, severe, without psychotic features (F33.2). He meets criteria for a second major depressive episode, severe, without psychotic features. The MDQ is negative and the interview finds no past hypomanic or manic episode: the earlier period of intense work did not include reduced need for sleep, elation or irritability, so bipolar disorder is not diagnosed, but he should be watched for activation once an antidepressant starts. The tests exclude the common medical causes. Severe depression with a sustained stressor and passive thoughts of death in an older man needs close follow-up, but he has no intent or plan, good supports and a safety plan, so outpatient care is appropriate. [S]

Persecution and surveillance (Z60.5). His concern about being watched is plausible, specific and consistent with his circumstances; it is not a delusion, and labelling it as paranoia would be a diagnostic error of the kind documented more often in Black patients. Depression, rather than psychosis, explains his presentation, and the persecution is a real stressor that therapy should address directly. [S]

text.paragraph: Data reviewed: Dr. Bankole-Ashworth's intake note, safety assessment and results: PHQ-9 22 (item 9 scored 1), GAD-7 12, MoCA 28; blood count, sodium 140, potassium 4.2, creatinine 1.05 mg/dL, glucose 92, calcium 9.4, TSH 1.8, vitamin B12 420, folate 9.5, morning testosterone 420 ng/dL and A1c 5.6%, all normal; HIV and syphilis tests negative. Structured diagnostic interview today (mood, psychosis, anxiety, trauma and substance modules) and the Mood Disorder Questionnaire (5 of 13 items, not in one period). [S]

list.item: Outpatient care with the written safety plan, locked medicines, no firearm, the 988 Suicide & Crisis Lifeline, and a C-SSRS screen at every visit; admission if thoughts become active, with intent or a plan. [S]
Behavioral activation weekly for about sixteen sessions with a psychologist he chooses, then CBT if needed. [S]

Sertraline 50 mg each morning, 100 mg at two weeks, then up to 200 mg by eight weeks as tolerated; sodium at about six weeks; PHQ-9 at every visit, with response as a 50 percent fall and remission as a score below 5. [S]

If the PHQ-9 falls by less than a quarter after an adequate trial (at least four to eight weeks at an adequate dose), switch to an SNRI such as venlafaxine extended-release up to 225 mg, with blood pressure checks and 30-day supplies. [S]

If a second adequate trial brings only a partial response, treat it as treatment-resistant depression: augmentation with aripiprazole (with metabolic and movement monitoring) or lithium, or ECT, rTMS or esketamine. [S]

ECT is not indicated now; it is indicated first for psychotic depression, refusal of food or drink, or acute suicidal risk, and is a choice for treatment-resistant depression. If chosen, it should be given with his own informed consent, under general anesthesia with a muscle relaxant, usually right unilateral with an ultrabrief pulse, two or three times a week in a defined course, with the MoCA repeated before and during the course, and with his right to stop at any time. [S]
Repeat the MDQ and review the diagnosis if he develops elation, reduced need for sleep or racing thoughts. [S]
Explain how his record is protected and keep the psychiatric notes to what care requires. [S]

Discussed with Dr. Bankole-Ashworth the same morning; he will prescribe and coordinate the psychologist and social worker, and I am available by phone for each medicine change. Mr. Robeson agreed to the plan and asked that no treatment, especially ECT, be given without his own agreement; he was assured that it would not be. [S]
Follow-up: Telephone review with Dr. Bankole-Ashworth at each medicine change, and a further consultation if two antidepressant trials fail or if risk rises. [S]
